passages.source_text: δεῖ δὲ καὶ ἐν ταῖς εὐχαῖς τὸ θεῷ προσπεφευγέναι ὁμολογεῖν, καὶ διαμαρτύρεσθαι τὴν τοῦ δαίμονος οὐκ ἀπείθειαν, ἀλλὰ βραδυτῆτα. πάντα γὰρ τῷ πιστεύοντι γίνεται, ἀπιστοῦντι δὲ οὐδέν. ὅθεν αὐτοὶ οἱ δαίμονες, εἰδότες ὧν ἐπικρατοῦσιν τῆς πίστεως τὴν ποσότητα, ἀναλογοῦσαν ἐπιμετροῦσιν αὐτῶν τὴν ἐπιμονήν. διὰ τοῦτο τοῖς ἀπιστοῦσιν ἐπιμένουσιν, τοῖς δὲ δυσπίστοις ἐνβραδύνουσιν, τοῖς δὲ παντάπασιν πιστεύσασι καὶ εὖ πράττουσιν οὐδὲ πρὸς ῥοπὴν ὥρας συνεῖναι δύνανται. ἡ γὰρ ψυχὴ τῇ πρὸς θεὸν πίστει ὡς εἰς ὕδατος φύσιν τραπεῖσα τὸν δαίμονα ὡς σπινθῆρα πυρὸς ἀποσβέννυσιν. κάματος οὖν ἐστὶν ἑκάστῳ ἐννοηθῆναι τὴν τοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ δαίμονος φυγήν. ἀνακιρνάμενοι γὰρ ταῖς ψυχαῖς, ὅπως τις τῆς αὐτοῦ σωτηρίας ἀμελήσῃ, ἐνθυμήσεις πρὸς ἃ βούλονται ὑποβάλλουσιν εἰς τὸν ἑκάστου νοῦν.

ὅθεν πολλοὶ οὐκ εἰδότες πόθεν ἐνεργοῦνται, ταῖς τῶν δαιμόνων κακαῖς ὑποβαλλομέναις ἐπινοίαις ὡς τῷ τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτῶν λογισμῷ συντίθενται. διὸ πρὸς τοὺς σώζειν αὐτοὺς δυναμένους ἐλθεῖν ὀκνηρότεροι γίνονται καὶ τοὺς ὑπ’ αὐτῶν τῶν ἐνεδρευόντων δαιμόνων ἀναλισκόμενοι ἀγνοοῦσιν. ὑπὸ μὲν οὖν τῶν ταῖς ψυχαῖς αὐτῶν ἐνδομυχούντων δαιμόνων ἐπιδίδοται αὐτοῖς ἐνθυμεῖσθαι ὡς οὐ δαίμονος ἐνοχλοῦντος, ἀλλὰ σωματικῆς νόσου (οἷον ἢ ὕλης δριμείας ἢ χολῆς ἢ φλέγματος ἢ αἵματος ἀμετρίας ἢ μήνιγγος φλεγμονῆς ἢ ἄλλου τινός) . . . . εἰ δὲ καὶ τοῦτο ἦν, οὐδὲ αὐτὸ ἀπήλλακται δαίμονος εἶδος εἶναι. ἡ γὰρ καθόλου καὶ γεώδης ψυχή, αἰτία πάντων βρωτῶν διικνουμένη, ὑπὸ τῆς πλείονος τροφῆς ἐπὶ πλεῖον προσληφθεῖσα, αὐτὴ μὲν ὡς συγγενεῖ ἐνοῦται τῷ πνεύματι (ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἀνθρώπου ψυχή), τὸ δὲ τῆς τροφῆς ὑλῶδες τῷ σώματι ἑνωθὲν ὡς δεινὸς αὐτῷ ὑπαλείφεται ἰός. διὸ ἐπὶ πάντων καλὸν ἡ αὐτάρκεια.

τινὲς δὲ τῶν κακούργων δαιμόνων ἄλλως ἐνεδρεύουσιν, τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐδὲ ὅτι εἰσὶν ἐνφαίνοντες, ὅπως ἡ κατ’ αὐτῶν σπουδὴ μὴ γένηται, εὐκαίρως δὲ ὀργῆς προφάσει, ἔρωτος ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς ἤτοι ξίφει ἢ βρόχῳ ἢ κρημνῷ ἢ ἑτέρῳ τινὶ τὸ σῶμα αἰφνιδίως ἐνυβρίζουσιν, καὶ εἰς τέλος κολασθησομένας καθιστᾶσιν τῶν ἀνακεκραμένων τὰς ἠπατημένας αὐτοῖς ψυχάς, ὡς ἔφαμεν, εἰς τὸ καθάρσιον χωρήσαντες πῦρ. ἄλλοι δὲ ἄλλως ἐνεδρευόμενοι οὐ προσίασιν ἡμῖν, ταῖς τῶν κακούργων δαιμόνων ἐνθυμήσεσιν ἀπατώμενοι ὡς ὑπὸ μὲν τῶν θεῶν αὐτῶν ταῦτα πάσχοντες διὰ τὴν πρὸς αὐτοὺς ἀμέλειαν, θυσίαις δὲ αὐτοὺς διαλλάσσειν δυνάμενοι, καὶ ὅτι μὴ χρὴ αὐτοὺς ἡμῖν προσιέναι, ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον φεύγειν καὶ μισεῖν. καὶ ὁμῶς μισοῦσιν καὶ φεύγουσιν τοὺς μᾶλλον ἐλεῶντας καὶ ἐπ’ εὐεργεσίᾳ αὐτοὺς διώκοντας.

μισοῦντες οὖν καὶ φεύγοντες ἡμᾶς ἐνεδρεύονται, οὐκ εἰδότες πόθεν αὐτοῖς τὰ ἐναντία τῇ αὐτῶν σωτηρίᾳ φρονεῖν γίνεται· οὔτε γὰρ ἡμεῖς αὐτοὺς μὴ βουλομένους πρὸς σωτηρίαν νεῦσαι βιάσασθαι δυνάμεθα (ἐπεὶ μὴ τοσαύτην νῦν κατ’ αὐτῶν ἔχομεν ἐξουσίαν) οὔτε αὐτοὶ ἀφ’ ἑαυτῶν τὴν κακὴν τοῦ δαίμονος ἐνθύμησιν νοῆσαι δύνανται (οὐ γὰρ ἴσασιν ὅθεν αὐτοῖς αἱ τῶν κακῶν ἐνθυμήσεις ὑποβάλλονται). εἰσὶν δὲ οὗτοι, οὓς οἱ δαίμονες καθ’ ἃς βούλονται μορφὰς ἐπιφαινόμενοι φοβοῦσιν. ἔσθ’ ὅτε δὲ καὶ τοῖς νοσοῦσιν θεραπείας συντάσσουσιν, καὶ οὕτως τοῖς προηπατημένοις θεῶν δόξαν ἀποφέρονται καὶ τοῦ δαίμονας εἶναι τοὺς πολλοὺς λανθάνουσιν, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ἡμᾶς τοὺς εἰδότας αὐτῶν τὸ μυστήριον τίνος ἕνεκα τοιαῦτα πράττουσιν, ἑαυτοὺς κατ’ ὄναρ καθ’ ὧν τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἔχουσι μεταμορφοῦντες. καὶ οὓς μὲν φοβοῦσιν, οἷς δὲ χρηματίζουσιν καὶ θυσίας ἀπαιτοῦσιν καὶ συνεστιᾶσθαι κελεύουσιν, ἵνα αὐτῶν τὰς ψυχὰς συνπίνωσιν.

ὡς γὰρ οἱ δεινοὶ ὄφεις τοῖς αὐτῶν πνεύμασιν τοὺς στρουθοὺς ἐπισπῶνται, οὕτω καὶ αὐτοὶ τοὺς μεταλαμβάνοντας τῆς αὐτῶν τραπέζης (διά γε τῶν βρωτῶν καὶ ποτῶν ἀνακραθέντες αὐτῶν τῷ νῷ) εἰς τὸ ἴδιον αὐτῶν ἐπισπῶνται βούλημα, μεταμορφοῦντες ἑαυτοὺς κατ’ ὄναρ κατὰ τὰς τῶν ξοάνων ἰδέας, ἵνα τὴν πλάνην αὐξήσωσιν. τὸ γὰρ ξόανον οὔτε ζῷόν ἐστιν οὔτε θεῖον ἔχει πνεῦμα, ὁ δὲ ὀφθεὶς δαίμων τῇ μορφῇ ἀπεχρήσατο. πόσοις κατ’ ὄναρ ὁμοίως ἄλλοις ὤφθησαν καὶ ὕπαρ συναντήσαντες ἀλλήλοις πρὸς τὸ κατ’ ὄναρ ἀντιβάλλοντες οὐ συνεφώνησαν; ὥστε οὐκέτι ὄναρ ἐπιφανείη ἐκεῖνό ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ ἢ δαίμονός ἐστιν ἢ ψυχῆς τὰ ἐπιγενήματα τοῖς παρίᾳ φόβοις καὶ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἀποδιδούσης τὰς ἰδέας· ἢ γὰρ φόβῳ τὸν νοῦν πληγεῖσα, διὰ ὀνείρων τὰς ἰδέας ἀποκυΐσκει. εἰ δὲ τὰ ξόανα οἴεσθε ὡς ἔνπνοα ὑπάρχοντα τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐνεργεῖν δύνασθαι, ἐπὶ ζυγοῦ ἐπιστήσαντες αὐτά, ἴσου ὄντος τοῦ κανόνος, τὸ ἀντίρροπον ἐπὶ τῆς ἑτέρας πλάστιγγος θέντες, ἀξιώσατε αὐτὰ ἢ ὁλκότερα γενέσθαι ἢ κουφότερα, καὶ οὕτως ἐὰν γένηται, ἔνπνοά ἐστιν· ἀλλ’ οὐ γίνεται· εἰ δὲ ἔσται, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν. καὶ γὰρ δακτύλῳ δαίμονος τοῦτο γενέσθαι δύναται. καὶ σκώληκες κινοῦνται, καὶ θεοὶ οὐ λέγονται.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: And in prayers one must also confess that one has taken refuge in God and solemnly affirm that, on the demon’s part, it is not disobedience but delay. For everything comes to pass for the one who believes, but nothing for the one who does not believe. Hence the demons themselves, knowing the quantity of faith possessed by those whom they overpower, allot a proportionate measure of their own persistence. For this reason they persist with those who do not believe, linger with those who have difficulty believing, but cannot remain even for an instant with those who have believed completely and act well. For the soul, having been turned by faith toward God as though into the nature of water, extinguishes the demon like a spark of fire. It is therefore difficult for each person to recognize the flight of the demon within them. For by blending themselves with souls, the demons suggest to each person’s mind thoughts directed toward whatever they wish, so that the person neglects their own salvation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that one has taken refuge in God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect infinitive presents recourse to God as an accomplished act with a continuing state.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not disobedience but delay
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast concerns the demon’s delayed departure rather than outright refusal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the quantity of faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording explicitly presents faith as possessing a measurable degree or amount.

lexical_decisions.chosen: linger with those who have difficulty believing
lexical_decisions.rationale: δύσπιστος denotes difficulty or reluctance in believing, distinguished here from outright unbelief.

lexical_decisions.chosen: It is therefore difficult
lexical_decisions.rationale: κάματος literally denotes labor or weariness and here characterizes recognition as laborious or difficult.

passages.text: Hence many, not knowing where the power acting on them comes from, assent to the evil notions suggested by demons as though they were the reasoning of their own soul. Therefore they become more reluctant to go to those capable of saving them; and while being consumed by the very demons lying in wait for them, they fail to recognize those people. The demons lurking in the innermost recesses of their souls prompt them to suppose that it is not a demon troubling them but a bodily disease—such as acrid matter, bile, phlegm, an imbalance of blood, inflammation of the meninges, or something else—. . . . But even if this were so, not even that is exempt from being a form of demon. For the universal and earthy soul, which extends through all foods as their cause, when taken in to a greater extent through more abundant food, itself unites with the spirit as something kindred to it—the spirit being the soul of a human being—while the material portion of the food, once united with the body, is smeared upon it like a terrible poison. Therefore self-sufficiency is good in everything.

lexical_decisions.chosen: where the power acting on them comes from
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive verb describes an agency or power operating upon them, while πόθεν asks its source.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τοὺς ὑπ’ αὐτῶν τῶν ἐνεδρευόντων δαιμόνων ἀναλισκόμενοι ἀγνοοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: and while being consumed by the very demons lying in wait for them, they fail to recognize those people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative τοὺς is taken anaphorically as the object of ἀγνοοῦσιν, referring to the people capable of saving them; ἀναλισκόμενοι describes those who fail to recognize their prospective helpers.

lexical_decisions.chosen: demons lurking in the innermost recesses
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνδομυχέω depicts dwelling or hiding deep within an interior recess.

lexical_decisions.chosen: acrid matter
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the medical list ὕλη denotes bodily matter or material; “acrid humor” is possible but would impose a more specific technical sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being a form of demon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase categorizes the proposed bodily condition as a manifestation or kind of demon within the author’s framework.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ γὰρ καθόλου καὶ γεώδης ψυχή
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the universal and earthy soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: καθόλου and γεώδης characterize this soul as universal and earth-associated; “general terrestrial soul” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: self-sufficiency
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this dietary context αὐτάρκεια may imply contentment, sufficiency, or moderation, but the main rendering retains its broader sense.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ τοὺς ὑπ’ αὐτῶν τῶν ἐνεδρευόντων δαιμόνων ἀναλισκόμενοι ἀγνοοῦσιν
source_issues.issue: The placement of the accusative τοὺς before the intervening participial phrase is marked, but it can defensibly function as an anaphoric object of ἀγνοοῦσιν, referring back to τοὺς σώζειν αὐτοὺς δυναμένους. The main text follows that reading. If τοὺς is not anaphoric, the construction becomes irregular and deletion might be conjectured, but no correction is adopted.

source_issues.source_quote: ἢ ἄλλου τινός) . . . . εἰ δὲ καὶ τοῦτο ἦν
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a lacuna marked by exactly four dots. Its content is unavailable, and no restoration has been supplied; the same four-dot gap remains explicit in the translation.

passages.text: Some of the wicked demons lie in wait in another way. At first they do not even reveal that they exist, so that no effort against them may arise; but at an opportune moment, under the pretext of anger, erotic passion, or something else, they suddenly assault the body by a sword, a noose, a precipice, or some other means. And, having entered the purifying fire, as we said, they bring it about that the deceived souls of those who have been mingled with them will be punished to the end. Others, being ambushed in another way, do not approach us, because they are deceived by the thoughts of the wicked demons into supposing that they suffer these things from their own gods because of their neglect toward them, that they can reconcile those gods through sacrifices, and that they must not approach us but, on the contrary, must flee and hate us. And all the same, they hate and flee those who have greater compassion for them and pursue them in order to benefit them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐδὲ ὅτι εἰσὶν ἐνφαίνοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: At first they do not even reveal that they exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὴν ἀρχήν can mean “at the beginning” or idiomatically “at all”; the subsequent reference to an opportune occasion favors a temporal contrast.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὀργῆς προφάσει, ἔρωτος ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: under the pretext of anger, erotic passion, or something else
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔρως here denotes passionate or erotic desire, while πρόφασις presents these emotions as pretexts or occasions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they suddenly assault the body
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνυβρίζω conveys violent mistreatment or outrage against the body.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they bring it about that ... will be punished to the end
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future passive participle κολασθησομένας gives the punishment prospective force. εἰς τέλος may mean “to the end,” “completely,” or, in some contexts, “forever”; the source-transparent wording leaves its extent unresolved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having entered the purifying fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: χωρήσαντες is nominative masculine plural and most directly resumes the demons as grammatical subject. A contextual association with the people mingled with them is possible despite the case difference.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And all the same
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμῶς can mean “alike” or “all the same”; the latter preserves the ironic contrast with the compassion shown to them.

passages.text: Thus, by hating and fleeing us, they are ensnared, not knowing from what source it comes about that they think things contrary to their own salvation. For neither can we compel them, when they are unwilling, to incline toward salvation—since we do not now have such authority over them—nor can they by themselves recognize the demon’s evil thought, for they do not know from where the thoughts of evil are suggested to them. These are the people whom the demons terrify by appearing in whatever forms they wish. Sometimes they also prescribe treatments for the sick, and in this way they gain among those already deceived a reputation as gods and conceal from most people that they are demons—but not from us, who know their secret, the reason why they do such things, transforming themselves in dreams against those over whom they have authority. Some they terrify; to others they issue oracles, demand sacrifices, and command them to share a feast, so that they may drink down their souls along with them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to incline toward salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: νεύω depicts leaning, inclining, or signaling assent rather than merely moving physically.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the demon’s evil thought
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνθύμησις can denote a thought, consideration, or inward suggestion; the genitive identifies the demon as its source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: prescribe treatments
lexical_decisions.rationale: συντάσσω can mean arrange or prescribe, and θεραπεία here refers to treatment or care for the sick.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they gain ... a reputation as gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: δόξα here is reputation or estimation, while θεῶν expresses the status attributed to them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑαυτοὺς κατ’ ὄναρ καθ’ ὧν τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἔχουσι μεταμορφοῦντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: transforming themselves in dreams against those over whom they have authority
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first κατά marks the dream setting; the second can bear the adversative sense “against.” It may alternatively refer more generally to those subject to their power.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they may drink down their souls along with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The souls are the accusative object of συνπίνωσιν. The compound evokes drinking together at the feast while portraying the demons as consuming the participants’ souls.

passages.text: For just as formidable snakes draw sparrows toward themselves with their breaths, so these demons also draw those who partake of their table into their own will, having mixed themselves into their minds through the food and drink. They transform themselves in dreams according to the likenesses of the carved images in order to increase the deception. For the carved image is neither a living creature nor does it possess a divine spirit; rather, the demon that was seen made use of its form. To how many others have they similarly appeared in dreams, and did those people not agree when they met one another while awake and compared what was in the dream? Consequently, what might appear is no longer a dream; rather, it either belongs to a demon or consists of the products of a soul that assigns the forms to fears in the cheek and to desire. For, alternatively, when its mind has been struck by fear, it gives birth to the forms through dreams. But if you think that the carved images, since they are animate, can perform such things, set them on a balance when its beam is level, place the counterweight on the other pan, and call upon them to become either heavier or lighter. If that happens, they are animate; but it does not happen. If, however, it should happen, such a thing is in that way a god. For even this can happen by the finger of a demon. Worms also move, and they are not called gods.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ δεινοὶ ὄφεις τοῖς αὐτῶν πνεύμασιν τοὺς στρουθοὺς ἐπισπῶνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: formidable snakes draw sparrows toward themselves with their breaths
lexical_decisions.rationale: πνεύματα here are the snakes’ breaths or exhalations, and στρουθοί most naturally denotes sparrows or small birds.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διά γε τῶν βρωτῶν καὶ ποτῶν ἀνακραθέντες αὐτῶν τῷ νῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: having mixed themselves into their minds through the food and drink
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνακραθέντες portrays the demons as becoming mixed with the participants’ mind by means of what is eaten and drunk.

lexical_decisions.chosen: according to the likenesses of the carved images
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξόανον is a carved cult image, often wooden, while ἰδέαι here are its visible forms or likenesses.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πόσοις κατ’ ὄναρ ὁμοίως ἄλλοις ὤφθησαν καὶ ὕπαρ συναντήσαντες ἀλλήλοις πρὸς τὸ κατ’ ὄναρ ἀντιβάλλοντες οὐ συνεφώνησαν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: To how many others have they similarly appeared in dreams, and did those people not agree when they met one another while awake and compared what was in the dream?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clauses are coordinated by καί, and οὐ συνεφώνησαν is retained as a negative question expecting agreement rather than converted into an assertion that they disagreed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when they met one another while awake
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὕπαρ contrasts waking experience with what was experienced in a dream.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥστε οὐκέτι ὄναρ ἐπιφανείη ἐκεῖνό ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Consequently, what might appear is no longer a dream
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes ἐκεῖνο as the subject associated with optative ἐπιφανείη and ὄναρ as the predicate of ἐστιν. The construction is irregular, and an alternative sense is that the appearance is no longer merely a dream apparition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς παρίᾳ φόβοις καὶ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἀποδιδούσης τὰς ἰδέας
lexical_decisions.chosen: that assigns the forms to fears in the cheek and to desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verified παρίᾳ is provisionally read as a dative singular meaning “cheek,” comparable to παρειά, and construed as a locative or somatic dative associated with φόβοις: “fears in the cheek,” perhaps fears manifested facially. This supplies literal English for the printed word, but the attachment and contextual sense remain highly uncertain.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ γὰρ φόβῳ τὸν νοῦν πληγεῖσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: For, alternatively, when its mind has been struck by fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: “For” represents γάρ and “alternatively” represents the printed disjunctive ἢ without adopting the conjectural replacement ἡ.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it gives birth to the forms through dreams
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποκυΐσκω uses the image of conceiving or giving birth, here applied to the soul’s production of dream forms.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ δὲ ἔσται, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: If, however, it should happen, such a thing is in that way a god
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected text and punctuation present this as a statement. The surrounding reductio could support hearing it rhetorically, but a question is not imposed on the main text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by the finger of a demon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the concrete image of a demon’s finger as the means by which the apparent change could be produced.

source_issues.source_quote: ὥστε οὐκέτι ὄναρ ἐπιφανείη ἐκεῖνό ἐστιν
source_issues.issue: The relation of optative ἐπιφανείη, neuter ἐκεῖνο, and ἐστιν is syntactically irregular and permits more than one division. The main rendering treats ἐκεῖνο as what might appear and ὄναρ as the predicate, while an alternative understands the phrase more generally as denying that the appearance is merely a dream apparition.

source_issues.source_quote: τοῖς παρίᾳ φόβοις καὶ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἀποδιδούσης τὰς ἰδέας
source_issues.issue: The image-verified print παρίᾳ can provisionally be identified as a dative singular meaning “cheek,” comparable to παρειά. The main text therefore construes it literally as a locative or somatic dative inserted within τοῖς ... φόβοις, yielding “fears in the cheek.” Although this accounts for every printed word in English, the construction is marked and does not yield a secure contextual sense beside καὶ ἐπιθυμίᾳ. Corruption remains plausible, but no supported correction has been established or adopted. Because the phrase’s meaning remains unresolved beyond this strained provisional construal, publication remains blocked.

source_issues.source_quote: ἢ γὰρ φόβῳ τὸν νοῦν πληγεῖσα
source_issues.issue: The printed ἢ is retained in the main text as a disjunctive represented by “alternatively,” with γάρ represented by “For.” The conjecture ἡ would instead make the feminine article directly introduce πληγεῖσα and yield, “For the soul, when struck in its mind by fear,” but that conjecture is not adopted as the supplied reading.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἡ γὰρ φόβῳ τὸν νοῦν πληγεῖσα

"translation_policy_text": "# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
